title: Pairs Where the Left Beats Double
statement:
You get an integer array nums. Count the pairs of positions i < j where the earlier value is strictly greater than twice the later one: nums[i] > 2 · nums[j].

Values can be negative and can be as large as a 32-bit integer, so 2 · nums[j] may not fit in 32 bits.

examples.why: 5 > 4 and 5 > 2 count. The pair 2, 1 does not: 2 is equal to twice 1, not greater.
Twice −3 is −6, and −4 > −6. Doubling a negative number makes it smaller.
Every earlier value is smaller than the later ones, so no pair works.

hints: Checking every pair is O(n²). If the later half of the array were sorted, could you count the matches for one earlier value faster?
Merge sort splits the array into a left and a right half. Every pair is either inside one half or has i in the left half and j in the right half.
With both halves sorted, walk a pointer through the right half: as the left value grows, the number of right values with left > 2 · right only grows. Count, then merge as usual.

explain.intuition:
The order constraint i < j is what makes this hard: you cannot just sort the array. Merge sort keeps exactly the information you need. When it merges two sorted halves, every value in the left half came from earlier in the array than every value in the right half. So the cross pairs can be counted on sorted data.

On two sorted halves the count is a two-pointer sweep. For each left value, in increasing order, advance a pointer through the right half while left > 2 · right[p]. Bigger left values can only pass more right values, so the pointer never moves back. Pairs inside each half were already counted by the recursive calls.
steps: Recursively sort and count the left half and the right half.
With both halves sorted, set p to the start of the right half.
For each value x in the left half, advance p while x > 2 · right[p], and add the number of right values passed so far.
Merge the two halves into sorted order.
Return the sum of the three counts.
pitfalls: Computing 2 · nums[j] in 32-bit integers. In languages with fixed-width ints it overflows; use 64-bit math.
Counting while merging, with the merge's own comparison. The merge compares x with y, but the count needs x with 2y, so it needs its own pass.
Using ≥ instead of >: the pair 2, 1 must not count.

solutions.title: Check every pair
solutions.idea: Two nested loops over i < j.

solutions.title: Merge sort with a counting pass
solutions.idea: Before merging two sorted halves, sweep them with two pointers to count cross pairs.

solutions.title: Fenwick tree over sorted values
solutions.idea: Walk right to left. For each value x, ask how many values already seen are below x / 2, then add x. Ranks come from one sorted copy and binary search.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def countSteepPairs(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        sorted_vals = sorted(set(nums))
        m = len(sorted_vals)
        tree = [0] * (m + 1)
        count = 0
        for x in reversed(nums):
            # seen values y with 2y < x
            k = bisect.bisect_left(sorted_vals, x / 2)
            while k > 0:
                count += tree[k]
                k -= k & -k
            j = bisect.bisect_left(sorted_vals, x) + 1
            while j <= m:
                tree[j] += 1
                j += j & -j
        return count
